topics.title: If, when and unless: real conditions
topics.summary: Zero and first conditionals for facts and likely futures.
notice: If you heat ice, it **melts**.
If it **rains** tomorrow, we**'ll stay** at home.
**Unless** you hurry, you'll miss the bus.
**When** I get home, I'll call you.

compare.a: If I see Ali, I'll tell him.
compare.b: When I see Ali, I'll tell him.
compare.note: A: maybe you will see him, maybe not. B: you are sure you will see him.

explain.en: Zero conditional (if + present, present) for things that are always true. First conditional (if + present, will + verb) for real, likely situations in the future. Do not use will after if, when, unless, as soon as, before, until: say 'If it rains', not 'If it will rain'. Unless = if not. When = you are sure it will happen.
explain.tr: if/when/unless/as soon as sonrasında will kullanılmaz: If it rains… unless = if not.

exercises.prompt: Which is natural?
options: If it will rain, we'll stay in.
If it rains, we'll stay in.

exercises.prompt: If you mix red and blue, you ___ (get) purple.
answers: get
exercises.why: A general fact: zero conditional, present + present.

exercises.prompt: If she passes the exam, she ___ (go) to university.
answers: will go
'll go

exercises.wrong: I'll call you as soon as I will arrive.
answers: I'll call you as soon as I arrive.
I will call you as soon as I arrive.
exercises.why: No will after as soon as.

exercises.wrong: Unless you don't study, you'll fail.
answers: Unless you study, you'll fail.
If you don't study, you'll fail.

exercises.prompt: Which speaker is sure the meeting will finish?
options: If the meeting finishes early, I'll join you.
When the meeting finishes, I'll join you.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite with 'unless': 'If you don't leave now, you'll be late.'
answers: Unless you leave now, you'll be late.
Unless you leave now, you will be late.
You'll be late unless you leave now.
You will be late unless you leave now.
exercises.why: Unless + positive verb = if + negative verb.

exercises.answer: If you need help, I'll be in my office.
alts: I'll be in my office if you need help.

exercises.prompt: Find the unnatural sentence.
options: Water freezes if the temperature drops below zero.
I'll wait here until you come back.
If I will have time, I'll visit you.
exercises.why: If I have time, I'll visit you.

exercises.prompt: Finish this sentence about your plans: 'If I have free time this weekend, …'
exercises.hint: Use will (or might) + verb in the result.
exercises.model: If I have free time this weekend, I'll visit my grandparents.

topics.title: Unreal present: second conditional and wish
topics.summary: Imagining a different present: If I had…, I wish I were…
notice: If I **had** more time, I **would learn** the piano.
If I **were** you, I**'d take** the job.
I **wish** I **lived** near the sea.
I wish I **could** speak Japanese.

compare.a: If I win the lottery, I'll buy a house.
compare.b: If I won the lottery, I'd buy a house.
compare.note: A sounds like you think winning is realistic. B is imaginary: it probably won't happen.

explain.en: Second conditional (if + past simple, would + verb) for imaginary or unlikely situations now or in the future. The past form does not mean past time here. 'If I were you' is the usual way to give advice. Wish + past simple expresses a wish about the present (I wish I had a car = I don't have one). Wish + could for abilities.
explain.tr: Second conditional: if + V2, would + V1 (hayali durum). I wish + V2: şimdiki zaman için dilek.

exercises.prompt: If I ___ (be) rich, I would travel around the world.
answers: were
was
exercises.why: Unreal present: past form. 'Were' is preferred in formal English.

exercises.prompt: If she studied more, she ___ (get) better marks.
answers: would get
'd get

exercises.prompt: Giving advice:
options: If I am you, I will apologise.
If I were you, I'd apologise.
exercises.why: Advice: If I were you, I'd…

exercises.prompt: You don't have a car. You say:
options: I wish I have a car.
I wish I had a car.
exercises.why: Wish about the present: past simple.

exercises.wrong: If I would have more money, I would buy a bike.
answers: If I had more money, I would buy a bike.
If I had more money, I'd buy a bike.
I wish I could swim.

exercises.prompt: Which speaker thinks it is unlikely?
options: If I get the job, I'll move to Izmir.
If I got the job, I'd move to Izmir.

exercises.answer: What would you do if you lost your job?

exercises.prompt: Find the unnatural sentence.
options: I'd be happier if I lived closer to work.
If I knew the answer, I'd tell you.
If I had a dog, I will walk it every day.
exercises.why: Second conditional result: I would walk it.

exercises.prompt: IELTS Speaking style: If you could live in any country, where would you live and why?
exercises.model: If I could live anywhere, I'd live in Canada because I love nature and quiet cities.

topics.title: Because, because of, so, so that, to
topics.summary: Linking reasons, results and purposes correctly.
notice: I stayed at home **because** I was ill.
The match was cancelled **because of** the rain.
It was late, **so** we took a taxi.
I saved money **to buy** a laptop.
Speak slowly **so that** everyone can understand.

compare.note: Because + a clause (subject + verb). Because of + a noun phrase.

explain.en: Reason: because + clause; because of / due to + noun. Result: so + clause (It was cold, so I wore a coat). Purpose: to + verb or in order to + verb (I came here to study); so that + subject + can/could/will/would (I left early so that I could catch the train). For purpose, do not say 'for + verb': say 'to learn', not 'for learn'.
explain.tr: because + cümle, because of + isim. so = sonuç. to / in order to / so that = amaç; 'for + fiil' yanlış.

exercises.prompt: The flight was delayed ___ the storm.
answers: because of
due to
exercises.why: A noun phrase follows: because of/due to.

exercises.prompt: I went to the shop ___ buy some bread.
answers: to
in order to

exercises.prompt: Which is natural?
options: I'm learning English for get a better job.
I'm learning English to get a better job.
exercises.why: Purpose: to + verb, not for + verb.

exercises.prompt: Which is natural?
options: Because of it was expensive, I didn't buy it.
Because it was expensive, I didn't buy it.

exercises.wrong: I was tired, because I went to bed early.
answers: I was tired, so I went to bed early.
I went to bed early because I was tired.
exercises.why: Going to bed was the result: so.

exercises.wrong: She whispered so that nobody hear her.
answers: She whispered so that nobody could hear her.
She whispered so that nobody would hear her.

exercises.prompt: Join with 'so': 'It started to rain. We went inside.'
answers: It started to rain, so we went inside.
It started to rain so we went inside.

exercises.answer: He set an alarm so that he wouldn't oversleep.

exercises.prompt: Find the unnatural sentence.
options: Due to the strike, there were no buses.
I called her to say sorry.
She was happy because of she passed.

exercises.prompt: Why are you learning English? Write one sentence with 'to' or 'so that' and one with 'because'.
exercises.hint: Purpose: to + verb. Reason: because + clause.
exercises.model: I'm learning English to study abroad, because many good universities teach in English.

topics.title: Too, enough, so and such
topics.summary: Saying 'more than needed', 'as much as needed' and adding emphasis.
notice: This coffee is **too hot** to drink.
He isn't **old enough** to drive.
We don't have **enough time**.
It was **so cold** that the lake froze.
It was **such a good film** that I watched it twice.

compare.note: A: heavy, but maybe you can carry it. B: so heavy that there is a problem — you can't carry it.

explain.en: Too + adjective = more than is good or possible (too expensive to buy). Adjective + enough (big enough) but enough + noun (enough money). So + adjective/adverb (so tired); such + (a/an) + adjective + noun (such a nice day, such kind people). Both can be followed by 'that' + result.
explain.tr: too + sıfat = gereğinden fazla. sıfat + enough, enough + isim. so + sıfat; such + (a) + sıfat + isim.

exercises.prompt: Which is natural?
options: He's enough tall to play basketball.
He's tall enough to play basketball.

exercises.prompt: Which is natural?
options: It was so a beautiful day.
It was such a beautiful day.

exercises.prompt: I can't buy it. It's ___ expensive.
answers: too
exercises.why: More than you can pay: too.

exercises.prompt: Do we have ___ chairs for everyone?
answers: enough

exercises.wrong: The film was too good. I loved it.
answers: The film was very good. I loved it.
The film was so good. I loved it.
The film was really good. I loved it.
exercises.why: Too is negative (a problem). For something positive use very/so/really.

answers: They are such nice people.

exercises.prompt: Join with 'so … that': 'I was very tired. I fell asleep on the sofa.'
answers: I was so tired that I fell asleep on the sofa.
I was so tired I fell asleep on the sofa.

exercises.answer: The box is too heavy to lift.

exercises.prompt: Find the unnatural sentence.
options: She speaks so quickly that I can't follow.
There isn't enough milk.
The room isn't enough big.
exercises.why: big enough: The room isn't big enough.

exercises.prompt: Describe a problem in your city using too or not … enough.
exercises.hint: too + adjective / not + adjective + enough / not enough + noun.
exercises.model: There aren't enough parks, and the traffic is too heavy in the evenings.

topics.title: Question tags and adverbs of frequency
topics.summary: isn't it? / don't you? and where to put always, never, usually.
notice: It's cold today, **isn't it**?
You don't eat meat, **do you**?
She **always** arrives on time.
I **have never** been to Japan.
He **is usually** at home in the evening.

compare.a: You live near here, don't you?
compare.note: A sounds natural and friendly: you expect 'yes'. Learn tags as a pattern: positive sentence → negative tag, negative → positive.

explain.en: Question tags use the auxiliary from the sentence: positive sentence + negative tag (She's nice, isn't she?), negative sentence + positive tag (You can't swim, can you?). In the present/past simple use do/does/did (He works here, doesn't he?). 'I am' → aren't I? Adverbs of frequency (always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never) go before the main verb but after be and after the first auxiliary: I often walk / I'm often late / I've never seen.
explain.tr: Olumlu cümle → olumsuz etiket, olumsuz → olumlu. Sıklık zarfları ana fiilden önce, be ve yardımcı fiilden sonra gelir.

exercises.prompt: She plays the piano, ___ she?
answers: doesn't

exercises.prompt: They haven't arrived yet, ___ they?
answers: have
exercises.why: Negative sentence → positive tag with the same auxiliary.

exercises.prompt: Which tag is correct? 'I'm late, ___?'
options: amn't I
aren't I

exercises.prompt: Which is natural?
options: I go always to work by bus.
I always go to work by bus.
exercises.why: Frequency adverb before the main verb.

answers: She is never late.
She's never late.

exercises.wrong: You went to the party, wasn't you?
answers: You went to the party, didn't you?

exercises.answer: We usually have dinner at seven.

exercises.prompt: Find the unnatural sentence.
options: He can drive, can't he?
I have often thought about it.
Let's go, don't we?

exercises.prompt: 'It's a beautiful day, ___'
options: isn't it?
is it?
doesn't it?

exercises.prompt: Write two sentences about your habits using two different frequency adverbs.
exercises.hint: always / usually / often / sometimes / rarely / never.
exercises.model: I usually wake up at seven. I rarely drink coffee in the evening.

topics.title: Who, which, that, whose, where
topics.summary: Joining information about people, things and places.
notice: The woman **who** lives next door is a nurse.
This is the book **that** I told you about.
That's the café **where** we first met.
I have a friend **whose** father is a pilot.

compare.a: The man who I met was kind.
compare.b: The man I met was kind.
compare.note: Both are correct. When who/which/that is the object of the verb, you can leave it out.

explain.en: Use who (or that) for people, which (or that) for things, where for places, whose for possession. When the pronoun is the object of the clause (the film that I watched), you can omit it: the film I watched. Do not repeat the pronoun: 'the man who I met him' is wrong.
explain.tr: who = insan, which = şey, that = ikisi, where = yer, whose = sahiplik. Nesne konumundaysa zamir atılabilir; zamiri tekrar etme.

exercises.prompt: That's the hospital ___ I was born.
answers: where

exercises.prompt: I met a girl ___ brother plays for Galatasaray.
answers: whose

exercises.prompt: Which is natural?
options: The phone which I bought it is broken.
The phone which I bought is broken.

exercises.prompt: Which is natural?
options: She's the teacher which helped me.
She's the teacher who helped me.

exercises.wrong: This is the house who my grandfather built.
answers: This is the house that my grandfather built.
This is the house which my grandfather built.
This is the house my grandfather built.

exercises.prompt: Join with 'who': 'I have a cousin. She works in Dubai.'
answers: I have a cousin who works in Dubai.

exercises.answer: The film we watched last night was boring.
exercises.why: Object pronoun omitted: the film (that) we watched.

exercises.prompt: Find the unnatural sentence.
options: The car that I wanted was sold.
Is this the place where you work?
The people which I met were friendly.

exercises.prompt: Which word can be left out? 'The song (that) you sang was beautiful.'
options: that — it can be left out
that — it must stay
exercises.why: That is the object of 'sang', so it can go.

exercises.prompt: Describe a person who is important to you using who or whose.
exercises.hint: X is a person who… / X is someone whose…
exercises.model: My aunt is someone who always listens and whose advice is very practical.
